title: Well-Woman Visit and Preventive Care Periodicity
summary: At least one preventive visit per year from adolescence through life is recommended to deliver age- and risk-based screening, counseling, and immunizations; content varies by life stage rather than a fixed checklist.
key_points: WPSI: at least 1 preventive visit/year, adolescence through adulthood, no upper age limit
Services can be delivered across a series of visits, not only a single annual exam
Visit scope includes prepregnancy, prenatal, postpartum, and interconception care
Content is tailored by age, reproductive/pregnancy status, and individual risk factors
Core elements: psychosocial/physical function assessment, screening, immunizations, counseling, risk-factor review
No pelvic exam or Pap test is required at every annual visit for an asymptomatic average-risk patient
Annual visit is also the anchor point for cervical/breast/STI screening intervals and contraceptive counseling
management: Use the visit to reconcile which age/risk-based screenings (cervical, breast, STI, mental health, IPV) are due
Assess pregnancy intention and reproductive life plan at every visit in reproductive-age patients
Update immunizations (HPV, Tdap, influenza, COVID, others per age/risk)
Screen for IPV, depression/anxiety, and substance/tobacco use as part of routine psychosocial assessment
Tailor exam components (pelvic, breast) to symptoms and risk rather than performing by default
Document risk factors to set the interval for the next visit's focused screening
citations: WPSI, Well-Woman Preventive Visits (current edition — verify at womenspreventivehealth.org)

title: Breast Cancer Screening and Risk Assessment
summary: Average-risk women are offered mammography starting between ages 40-50 and continuing at least through age 74, while all women should have periodic breast-cancer risk assessment to identify candidates for genetic counseling/BRCA testing.
key_points: WPSI (average risk): initiate mammography no earlier than 40, no later than 50; at least biennial, up to annual
Continue screening mammography through at least age 74 in average-risk women
All women should undergo periodic risk assessment for breast/ovarian/tubal/peritoneal cancer, including family history and ancestry
Positive risk screen -> refer for formal genetic counseling before any genetic testing
High-risk women (known BRCA1/2, prior chest radiation, strong family history) need individualized surveillance beyond average-risk schedule
Validated risk-assessment tools (e.g., family-history-based models) help decide who needs referral, not who needs testing directly
Clinical breast exam and self-exam are not relied on as primary screening in asymptomatic average-risk women
management: Ask about personal and family history of breast/ovarian/tubal/peritoneal cancer at periodic visits
Use a structured tool/questionnaire to flag increased-risk patients for further workup
Refer positive screens to genetic counseling before ordering BRCA or other genetic testing
Shared decision-making on start age (40 vs 45-50) and interval (annual vs biennial) for average-risk patients
Escalate high-risk patients (BRCA+, prior thoracic radiation) to enhanced surveillance (earlier start, added MRI)
Reassess risk status periodically, since family history and personal risk can change over time
citations: WPSI, Breast Cancer Screening for Women at Average Risk (current edition — verify at womenspreventivehealth.org)
USPSTF, Breast Cancer: Screening; Risk Assessment, Genetic Counseling, and Genetic Testing for BRCA-Related Cancer (current edition — verify at uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org)

title: Screening for Interpersonal and Domestic Violence (IPV)
summary: Adolescent girls and women should be screened at least annually for interpersonal/domestic violence using a validated tool, with intervention or referral services available on-site when screens are positive.
key_points: WPSI: screen all adolescent and adult women at least annually for IPV/domestic violence
Definition spans physical, sexual, psychological, and reproductive coercion, stalking, and neglect
Higher-risk groups: pregnant patients, very young/older patients, LGBTQ+, those with disabilities or substance use
Validated brief screening tools exist with adequate sensitivity/specificity for clinical use
Screening should occur in private, without partner/family present, with a plan for safe disclosure
A positive screen requires same-visit safety assessment, not just documentation
management: Screen privately and confidentially at least annually, including during pregnancy
Use a brief validated screening instrument rather than an open-ended unscreened question alone
If positive, assess immediate safety and document using neutral, nonjudgmental language
Provide or refer for intervention services: counseling, advocacy, legal/social resources, shelters
Know mandatory reporting requirements and local resources before the encounter
Reassess at subsequent visits, since risk and disclosure can change over time
citations: WPSI, Screening and Counseling for Interpersonal and Domestic Violence (current edition — verify at womenspreventivehealth.org)

title: Screening for Anxiety and Depression in Women
summary: Women and adolescent girls age 13 and older, including during pregnancy and postpartum, should be periodically screened for anxiety and depression with validated instruments and a clear follow-up pathway for positive results.
key_points: WPSI: screen women/girls >=13 years for anxiety; USPSTF: screen all adults, including pregnant/postpartum, for depression
Perinatal screening instrument example: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)
General adult/anxiety tools cited include GAD-7, PHQ-4, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS)
Optimal screening interval is not firmly established; use clinical judgment for frequency
Screening must be paired with systems for accurate diagnosis and follow-up, not screening alone
Applies across pregnancy, postpartum, and nonpregnant adult life stages
management: Administer a validated combined or separate anxiety/depression tool at periodic/perinatal visits
Screen for depression and anxiety at intake prenatal visit, again later in pregnancy, and postpartum
Confirm diagnosis clinically (not on screening score alone) before initiating treatment
Initiate or refer for counseling/psychotherapy and consider pharmacotherapy per severity
Assess suicidality/safety whenever a screen is positive
Arrange follow-up visit to reassess symptom trajectory and treatment response
Coordinate with behavioral health/psychiatry for refractory or severe perinatal mood/anxiety disorders
citations: WPSI, Screening for Anxiety in Adolescent and Adult Women (current edition — verify at womenspreventivehealth.org)
USPSTF, Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (current edition — verify at uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org)

title: Preconception Counseling and Folic Acid Supplementation
summary: All women of reproductive potential should be counseled on reproductive life planning and take a daily folic acid supplement (0.4-0.8 mg) before conception and through early pregnancy to reduce neural tube defect risk.
key_points: USPSTF (Grade A): all women planning or capable of pregnancy take 0.4-0.8 mg folic acid daily
Begin supplementation at least 1 month before conception; continue through roughly first 2-3 months of pregnancy
Higher dose (up to 4 mg/day) considered for women with prior NTD-affected pregnancy or other high-risk factors
Preconception counseling (reproductive life plan, chronic disease optimization, teratogen review) is part of routine well-woman care, not a standalone USPSTF item
Address chronic conditions (diabetes, hypertension, thyroid, obesity), medications, and vaccinations before conception
Screen for and address substance/tobacco/alcohol use as part of preconception counseling
management: Ask every reproductive-age patient about pregnancy intention at routine visits
Prescribe/recommend daily folic acid 0.4-0.8 mg for anyone who could become pregnant
Escalate to high-dose folic acid (up to 4 mg) for prior NTD pregnancy or other elevated risk
Optimize chronic disease control (A1c, blood pressure, thyroid) before conception attempts
Review and adjust teratogenic medications ahead of planned pregnancy
Update vaccinations (e.g., MMR, varicella immunity) and address substance use before conception
Reinforce folic acid continuation into early pregnancy at the first prenatal visit
citations: USPSTF, Folic Acid for the Prevention of Neural Tube Defects: Preventive Medication (current edition — verify at uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org)
ACOG, Preconception Care Committee Opinion/Practice guidance (current edition — verify at acog.org)

title: Osteoporosis Screening
summary: Women 65 and older should be screened for osteoporosis with central DXA bone density testing; postmenopausal women under 65 are screened only if a risk-assessment tool shows elevated fracture risk.
key_points: USPSTF: screen all women >=65 years with central DXA BMD, with or without fracture risk assessment
Postmenopausal women <65: first check for risk factors, then use a clinical risk-assessment tool (e.g., FRAX) before deciding on DXA
Only proceed to DXA in the under-65 group if the risk tool indicates risk equivalent to a 65-year-old
2024 USPSTF update specifies central DXA (not peripheral/other bone measurement tests) as the screening method
Evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against routine screening in men
Secondary causes (steroid use, hyperthyroidism, malabsorption) warrant evaluation outside the routine screening pathway
management: Screen all women 65+ with central DXA regardless of risk factors
For postmenopausal women <65, apply a validated fracture risk tool before ordering DXA
Order DXA when risk-tool output meets the age-65-equivalent threshold
Counsel on calcium/vitamin D intake, weight-bearing exercise, and fall-prevention regardless of DXA result
Treat confirmed osteoporosis (T-score <=-2.5) or high fracture risk with pharmacotherapy per guidelines
Repeat DXA interval individualized to baseline T-score and risk profile, not a fixed universal interval
citations: USPSTF, Osteoporosis to Prevent Fractures: Screening (2024 update — verify at uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org)

title: Breastfeeding Support and Counseling
summary: Comprehensive lactation support — counseling, education, peer support, and breast-pump/supply access — should be provided across the antenatal, perinatal, and postpartum periods to help initiate and sustain breastfeeding.
key_points: WPSI: comprehensive lactation support services recommended across antenatal, perinatal, and postpartum periods
Services include consultation/counseling/education by clinicians and trained peer supporters
Covered equipment/supplies include double electric breast pumps and milk storage supplies
Access to a double electric pump should not require prior failure of a manual pump
Eligible lactation care providers include IBCLCs, breastfeeding counselors, midwives, APPs, and physicians
Support should begin prenatally, not only after delivery, to optimize initiation
management: Discuss breastfeeding intentions and address barriers at prenatal visits
Arrange lactation consultation proactively, not only after problems arise postpartum
Ensure access to a double electric breast pump and storage supplies without unnecessary prior-failure requirements
Provide anticipatory guidance on latch, milk supply, and common early complications (engorgement, mastitis)
Involve peer counselors/support groups for ongoing postpartum encouragement
Coordinate with pediatric care team for feeding/weight follow-up in the newborn period
citations: WPSI, Breastfeeding Services and Supplies (current edition — verify at womenspreventivehealth.org)

title: HPV Vaccination
summary: Routine HPV vaccination starts at age 11-12 (can begin at 9), with catch-up through age 26, and shared clinical decision-making for select adults age 27-45 who were not adequately vaccinated earlier.
key_points: ACIP: routine vaccination at age 11-12 years; series can start as early as age 9
Catch-up vaccination recommended through age 26 for anyone not previously fully vaccinated
Shared clinical decision-making applies to adults age 27-45 based on individual risk/benefit
2-dose schedule (0, 6-12 months) if series starts before the 15th birthday
3-dose schedule (0, 1-2, 6 months) if starting at/after age 15, or if immunocompromised
Vaccination is recommended regardless of prior HPV exposure, Pap/HPV test results, or sexual activity history
management: Recommend initiation at age 11-12 at well-child/adolescent visits; may start at 9
Use the 2-dose schedule for series started before age 15; switch to 3-dose if started at 15+ or immunocompromised
Offer catch-up vaccination to any unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated patient through age 26
Engage in shared decision-making for interested patients age 27-45 not previously fully vaccinated
Do not delay or withhold vaccination pending cervical cytology/HPV test results
Document doses given/needed and track completion at subsequent visits
citations: CDC/ACIP, Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccination: Recommendations (current edition — verify at cdc.gov)

title: Tobacco Use Screening and Cessation Counseling
summary: All adults, including pregnant patients, should be asked about tobacco use at every visit and offered tailored behavioral cessation support, with pregnancy-specific counseling intensity and caution on pharmacotherapy in pregnancy.
key_points: USPSTF (Grade A): ask all adults about tobacco use; provide cessation interventions for users
USPSTF (Grade A): ask all pregnant persons about tobacco use, advise cessation, and provide behavioral interventions
Pregnancy-tailored counseling (5-15 minutes, pregnancy-specific self-help materials) is more effective than brief advice alone
Evidence is insufficient (Grade I) on pharmacotherapy benefit/harm for tobacco cessation specifically in pregnancy
Nonpregnant adults: combine behavioral counseling with FDA-approved pharmacotherapy as first-line
Evidence is insufficient to recommend e-cigarettes for cessation in any adult population, including pregnant persons
Use the 5 A's framework (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange) to structure the encounter
management: Ask about tobacco use and document status at every visit, pregnant or not
Advise all users to quit with a clear, personalized message
Assess readiness/willingness to quit before choosing an intervention
In nonpregnant adults, assist with both behavioral counseling and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy
In pregnant patients, assist with augmented pregnancy-tailored behavioral counseling as first-line; use pharmacotherapy only with individualized risk-benefit discussion
Arrange follow-up to support quit attempts and address relapse
Avoid recommending e-cigarettes as a cessation method given insufficient evidence
citations: USPSTF, Tobacco Use in Adults and Pregnant Persons: Counseling and Interventions (current edition — verify at uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org)
